title: UTF8 SIMD scan & runtime slice profiling notes
content:
Summary and goal:

This is an experimental scratchpad capturing the UTF-8 scanning / tokenizer hot-path profiling we ran on the runtime slice scheduler. Goal: identify fast wins for small-request tail latency by pushing as much scanning work out of the Python-level loop as possible and evaluate whether SIMD-assisted scanning and batching across runtime-slices reduces median and p95 CPU time without increasing jitter.

Background/context:
- Recent customer reports (INF-1723) show p95 tokenization CPU for 32B requests spiking during bursty arrival patterns.
- Prior work focused on moving parts of tokenization into Rust/FFI; we still see ~50–120us per request spent inside Python framing + header parse + byte-scan for token boundaries on our x86 fleets.
- Hypothesis: the main contributor is byte-by-byte UTF-8 validation and boundary detection implemented in high-level code that triggers many short GIL-holding C calls, and our runtime slice scheduler causes preemptions that amplify jitter.

What we ran (quick notes on benches):
- Machines: c6i-like local perf nodes (8 vCPU), and an older aarch64 evaluation box for ARM checks.
- Baseline: current tokenizer path (python loop + memchr fallback) exercised with 1k synthetic small requests extracted from production traces (mix of ascii + non-ascii).
- SIMD prototype: a C++ microlib that implements a UTF-8 safety scan and newline/whitespace boundary search using AVX2/AVX512 where available, falling back to scalar for tails. Exposes a single buffer-scan API (offset, length) and returns boundary indexes in a small stack buffer to avoid heap allocs.
- Measurements collected: perf script + flamegraphs (kernel+user), py-spy samples, and a tiny eBPF trace for scheduler wakeups.

Key observations:
1) Median CPU per-request for naive path: ~110us on x86 baseline; p95 ~320us during bursts.
2) SIMD prototype (AVX2) reduced the buffer-scan portion by ~60–70% on ASCII-heavy payloads — end-to-end median fell to ~98us (9% improvement).
3) For mixed unicode inputs (≈20% multibyte chars), SIMD still wins but benefits shrink (~35% for scan portion) and total median improvement ~6%.
4) On ARM (NEON) microlib, scalar fallback performed comparably to AVX2 scalar for short buffers; NEON implementation needed more careful alignment handling — measured ~4% regression vs x86 AVX2 in this prototype.
5) The big regressor wasn't the scan itself in isolation but the interaction with the runtime slice scheduler: when the Python thread was preempted during short blocking C-call returns, we observed wake-up jitter that dominated p95. eBPF traces show many wakeups within ~200us windows correlated with Python GIL reacquire.

Detailed profiler notes:
- Flamegraphs show narrow high-frequency stacks: python framing -> tokenize_wrapper (c-extension) -> libc:memchr or our AVX scan -> return to python. The heavy tail has more scheduler syscalls (nanosleep/timerfd) in bursts.
- py-spy showed >60% of samples during tails landing in interpreter state while holding the GIL. This suggests the C-extension is not fully escaping GIL or we're reacquiring it frequently to build Python objects.
- perf counters: branch-mispredicts increased for AVX path on mixed unicode (unexpected), likely due to branchy continuation handling of partial multibyte sequences.

Tradeoffs and risks:
- Latency vs throughput: AVX scan improves single-request median but increases code complexity and maintenance. We need cross-platform builds (x86/ARM) and careful fallbacks.
- GIL interactions: if the C-extension holds the GIL, benefits are limited. Releasing the GIL during pure buffer-scan reduces interpreter blocking but requires careful error reporting and exception handling when returning indices to Python.
- Memory: returning lists of boundaries to Python can allocate; we used a preallocated small array and returned a compact slice length to avoid per-request heap churn. That reduced allocation time in microbenchmarks significantly.

Quick wins we can prototype next:
- Release GIL in C-extension for the scan-only path. Validate that exception-free code paths do not reacquire GIL until returning. Patch in PR: github:.../pull/48 is the initial branch.
- Replace memchr-heavy code paths with our vectorized memchr-like scan for ASCII-heavy requests and provide a runtime flag to enable/disable by model-route to avoid global rollout risks.
- Add a per-worker tokenizer scratch arena (stack-ish buffer) to avoid building Python objects for boundary arrays; surface results as (pointer,length) tuple rather than list when used internally by runtime.
- Scheduler mitigation: reduce slice preemption frequency for short-running tokenizer-critical paths. Experiment: bump runtime slice quantum for threads with high tokenize rates (config toggle), or use cooperative yielding instead of timerfd preemption for these workers.

Open experiments (TODOs):
- [ ] Complete AVX2 -> NEON port and build cross-architectural microbench comparisons (target: no-regression on aarch64).
- [ ] Implement GIL-release in C-extension and rerun py-spy flames to confirm interpreter sample reduction.
- [ ] End-to-end p95 test under synthetic bursty arrival (Poisson arrival with 500 qps spike); collect p50/p95/p99 and scheduler wakeups pre/post change.
- [ ] Small risk run: enable vectorized path behind feature flag on staging routes (2 replicas) and monitor p95 and OOM/GC metrics for 48h.

Notes for implementer (practical gotchas):
- Avoid writing the SIMD loop to assume 64-byte alignment; network buffers can be misaligned. Use unaligned loads where necessary or prologue/epilogue scalar handling.
- When releasing GIL, be careful with Python memoryviews/objects passed into C: copy vs pin semantics. We used a bytes pointer acquired from a C-level buffer protocol without creating a new bytes object to avoid copies.
- Branchless UTF-8 validation is tricky for overlong sequences; ensure we preserve strict validation to avoid accepting malformed input.

Proposed acceptance criteria for rollout:
- No increase in p99 by more than 5% for affected routes.
- Median reduction >= 5% for ascii-dominant workloads.
- No increase in GC/alloc churn observed in 48h staging run.

Slack / cross-team asks:
- Ask SRE: provide a staging bucket with traffic replay of 1.5x burst for 24h (ticket created: INF-1799).
- Ask runtime sched team: advise on safe runtime-quantum knobs and expected implications for throughput if we increase quantum for tokenizer threads.

Decision log (proposal):
- Short term: land SIMD-enabled scan behind flag + GIL-release in C-extension on staging.
- Medium term: integrate into tokenizer core and add route-level heuristics (ascii ratio) for auto-enable.

If you want to reproduce locally:
- linux x86 box with perf, build branch: rt-tokenizer/pr-48, run: ./bench/runner --trace-file traces/small-requests-1k.json --simd=on --workers=4 --burst=enabled
- Capture flamegraph: sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g -- ./bench/runner ... ; then perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > simd.svg

Attachments and experimental outputs (in the linked PR):
- simd_vs_scalar_1113.html (microbench results), simd_flame_svg/ - attached to PR 48.

Questions and open points:
- Should we prefer a Rust-based tokenizer FFI (simpler cross-platform story) or ship a tuned C++ microlib for ease of intrinsics use?
- Can the scheduler team expose a transient opt-out for preemption on specific worker classes?

End of notes.

-- aisha
(references: INF-1723, INF-1799, rt-tokenizer PR 48)
